fields.sections.0.h: Allegations of Refusal to Disclose Secret Court Rulings
fields.sections.1.h: FISA Court Surveillance Tool Issues Highlighted
fields.sections.2.h: Similar Past Cases and Persistent Problems
fields.sections.4.h: Credibility Issues with Surveillance Effectiveness Claims
fields.sections.5.h: Weakening of Surveillance Program Oversight System

fields.sections.7.h: Civil Society Organizations Urge Refusal of Reauthorization
fields.sections.0.ko: Two Democratic senators have pointed out that the Trump administration is not disclosing Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISA Court) rulings to Congress. They argue that the administration is intentionally hiding court rulings to obtain reauthorization of the Defense Communications Surveillance Program (Section 702). According to the administration's own regulations, rulings must be disclosed within 180 days of issuance, but this deadline passed on September 13 without disclosure.
fields.sections.1.ko: In March, the FISA Court raised issues with search filters that allowed intelligence analysts to extract communications of Americans without due process. The court determined that these tools constituted searches requiring constitutional protections for Americans and ordered them to be redesigned. Nevertheless, the court approved a one-year extension of the program, and the contents of this ruling were not disclosed to the public.
fields.sections.2.ko: A FISA Court ruling released last year revealed that the FBI's similar tool, the "Participant Filter," allowed queries of messages of individuals who contacted surveillance targets. In early this year, the Justice Department reported to the court that the tool had conducted indiscriminate searches, and the FBI suspended it before resuming it with a reauthorized version. This year's ruling is estimated to address broader issues than that.
fields.sections.3.ko: In April, bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee leadership requested the administration to disclose the ruling, and the Justice Department Attorney General promised in writing in July to disclose it by the 180-day deadline. However, the current Director of National Intelligence did not guarantee that the ruling would be disclosed before the Senate reauthorization vote. The administration claims it has provided the ruling to congressional members, but has not disclosed it to the general public.
fields.sections.4.ko: According to intelligence agency materials from March, the FBI surveillance search compliance rate claimed to reach 98.9%, and stated that Section 702 prevented a planned Taylor Swift concert terror attack in Vienna. However, a Justice Department Inspector General's report from October 2025 documented the compliance rate at 98.6% and stated it could not definitively conclude that FBI surveillance practices had been fully improved. This raises questions about the credibility of the administration's claims.
fields.sections.5.ko: FBI inspectors are known to review all surveillance searches, but the FBI Director abolished the internal inspector's office in May. Private surveillance officers were transferred to other departments, and searches conducted through the "Participant Filter" are missing from search records prior to 2025. The government privacy watchdog pointed out that these queries are untrackable.
fields.sections.6.ko: Senators who read the ruling hinted that its contents would significantly shift awareness of Americans' rights. There are also warnings that secret legal interpretations of Section 702, on which multiple administrations have relied, exist, and if disclosed, Americans would be surprised that Congress has debated this authority with insufficient information.
fields.sections.7.ko: 23 organizations, including the ACLU and conservative privacy protection groups, have urged congressional leaders to refuse reauthorization of Section 702 until the administration discloses legally mandated surveillance program information. This demonstrates that the absence of transparency is perceived as a program credibility issue.
fields.sections.8.ko: It is predicted that the administration may avoid separate discussion by including Section 702 reauthorization in the annual defense authorization bill. In 2023, the program was similarly extended for four months. The administration must respond to senators' demands by November 6, and the court's current authorization expires in March.
fields.caveat: This article was written primarily based on claims by Democratic senators and civil society organizations, and since an official statement from the administration was not provided at the time of writing, independent verification of the truth of the claims is necessary.
